part_title: Bedrock Agent Tracing and Evidence-Based Model Evaluation

scenes.title: Bedrock Agent tracing
scenes.narration: Start with the user's two-part question on the left: what is the return policy, and can you check my order status? Follow the architecture from left to right. The Bedrock agent plans how to address both requests. It retrieves policy documents from a knowledge base, then invokes an order-management action group to look up the shipment. Finally, it combines those two sources into a response. Below, the trace examples reveal how the steps were recorded. One entry identifies the retrieval action, another shows references such as Returns and Refunds Policy with relevance scores, and another records the order-status tool parameters and result. In the example, order A twelve three four five is marked shipped with an estimated delivery date. The useful question is not just whether the final answer sounds plausible, but which document and which tool result support it. A trace can explain the orchestration sequence and observations, but it does not expose the model's private internal reasoning tokens. For troubleshooting, compare the planned action, retrieved reference and tool observation to determine whether an incorrect answer came from retrieval, tool execution or response generation.

scenes.title: Foundation model evaluation criteria
scenes.narration: A good generative AI response needs more than correct grammar. Look at the example on the left: a user asks for three ways a company can reduce its carbon footprint, and the model proposes energy efficiency, renewable electricity and waste reduction. The scorecard on the right asks us to judge that answer from several angles. Accuracy checks whether the claims are true. Relevance asks whether all three suggestions address the actual request. Groundedness examines whether claims are supported by reliable evidence. Safety checks for harmful or misleading content. The next rows introduce latency, cost, robustness and adherence to the requested format. Notice the example targets: a latency below five seconds and a cost below two cents per query. Those are application-specific acceptance thresholds, not universal limits for every model. The pass-or-fail column turns general quality goals into a release decision. A model could be accurate but too expensive, or helpful but unsafe on an adversarial input. The lesson is to define a multidimensional rubric before choosing a foundation model and evaluate on real tasks, not one attractive demonstration.

scenes.title: Human evaluation workflow
scenes.narration: This slide shows how to obtain useful human judgment rather than collecting a few unstructured opinions. Follow the stages across the top. First, assemble representative prompts covering ordinary tasks, harder cases and edge conditions. Second, collect responses and hide the model identities so reviewers aren't influenced by brand expectations. Third, give multiple reviewers a consistent rubric and have them score each answer. Next, measure inter-rater agreement and investigate where their judgments differ. Then gather written feedback and use the findings to refine prompts or evaluation criteria. The lower example includes rubric dimensions such as helpfulness, correctness, safety and style on a one-to-five scale. One reviewer may say an answer is clear but misses an edge-case warning; another may find the tone good but request more structure. Those observations explain why a numeric score alone is incomplete. Human evaluation is particularly valuable for subtle harm, cultural context and whether an answer genuinely serves the user. But reviewers can be inconsistent, so calibration and repeated assessment are necessary. The practical output is evidence that helps the team decide what to improve before releasing the model.

scenes.title: Evaluation against benchmark datasets
scenes.narration: Now we're evaluating against a stable test set. Read the top workflow from left to right: create a curated prompt-and-answer dataset, hold out a fixed evaluation split, run the same prompts against the candidate model, compare responses using appropriate metrics, and track scores in a regression dashboard. The table below makes this concrete. It contains customer-support questions about returns, password reset, sign-up data and support hours. The model's answers appear beside references with groundedness scores. Notice that the return-policy answer receives a strong score, while an answer claiming support is available twenty-four seven conflicts with the reference business hours and scores poorly. The dashboard on the right tracks metrics such as groundedness, correctness and relevance across model versions. This prevents us from approving a new prompt or model based only on a few handpicked successes. One overall number can still hide failures for important user groups or high-risk prompts, so review scores by use case. Also protect the holdout set against accidental contamination. A good benchmark is representative, versioned and repeatable, making quality regressions visible before production.

scenes.title: Using another model as a judge
scenes.narration: Here we use one model to evaluate the answer produced by another. Follow the four steps along the top. A generator model receives a task and writes a response. The evaluator model then receives the original prompt, a reference answer when available, the generated response and a scoring rubric. It returns structured scores and an explanation. Humans inspect a sample of these evaluations to check whether the judge's reasoning follows the rubric. The example prompt asks for an explanation of photosynthesis. The generated answer is broadly correct, and the judge scores accuracy and completeness at four out of five, clarity at three and safety at five. Its explanation says the response could include more detail about chlorophyll and chloroplasts. That makes the score actionable. Look at the risks on the right: a judge can prefer certain writing styles, change behavior after model updates or share blind spots with the generator. The score is therefore not an independent fact-check by default. Calibrate the judge against trusted human examples and monitor disagreements. This method scales qualitative review, but human spot checks and task-specific benchmarks remain important.
